## Section 7.1 Learning Objectives {.center}

-   Identify a study design as having pairing or independent groups.

-   Identify a study design as paired using repeated measures or paired using matching.

# Review

## Chapter 5 Recap {.center}

Comparing two proportions:

-   [**Parameter:**]{.underline} $\pi_{Group\:1} - \pi_{Group\:2}$

-   [**Observed Statistic:**]{.underline} $\hat{p}_{Group\:1} - \hat{p}_{Group\:2}$

Hypotheses:

-   $H_0: \pi_{Group\:1} - \pi_{Group\:2} = 0$

-   $H_A: \pi_{Group\:1} - \pi_{Group\:2} >,<,\neq 0$

## Chapter 6 Recap {.center}

Comparing two means:

-   [**Parameter:**]{.underline} $\mu_{Group\:1} - \mu_{Group\:2}$

-   [**Observed Statistic:**]{.underline} $\bar{x}_{Group\:1} - \bar{x}_{Group\:2}$

Hypotheses:

-   $H_0: \mu_{Group\:1} - \mu_{Group\:2} = 0$

-   $H_A: \mu_{Group\:1} - \mu_{Group\:2} >,<,\neq 0$

## Comparing Two Groups {.center}

-   Comparing two proportions/means directly is just ONE way of comparing two groups

-   Can use paired design:

    -   Repeated measures

    -   Matched pairs

-   Either way, we must add "randomness"

# Example: Can you study with music blaring?

## Research Question {.center}

Does music with lyrics affect a student's ability to memorize words as opposed to music without lyrics?

## Experiment Setup {.center}

::: incremental
-   28 students selected to participate

-   Each student given a list of 5-letter words with 90 seconds to memorize as many as possible

-   Students either listen to music with OR without lyrics while doing so

-   Students write down as many words as they can remember
:::

## Experiment Setup {.center}

-   Explanatory variable: [**Music with or without lyrics**]{.fragment}

-   Response variable: [**Number of words memorized**]{.fragment}

. . .

We will look at three different ways of designing this study.

## 1. Independent Design {.center}

How we would design the experiment in chapter 6:

-   Randomly assign...

    -   14 students to listen to lyrics

    -   14 to listen to music with no lyrics

    -   This is how we add "randomness"

-   Then run the experiment

## 1. Independent Design {.center}

We refer to this as an **independent** design.

-   Individuals are independent from each other

-   Subjects can (and will) vary amongst each other

    -   No two individuals are exactly the same!

## 2. Repeated Measures Design {.center}

Design setup:

-   Each person listens to each kind of music

    -   First trial with one type of music

    -   Second trial with the other

-   Adding "randomness":

    -   It is randomly decided if a person listens to lyrics/no lyrics first

## 2. Repeated Measures Design {.center}

Now, variability is reduced!

-   Each person has been tested under each explanatory group

-   No subject to subject variability

## 3. Matched Pairs Design {.center}

-   Have students take a pre-test

-   Pair students basd on similar scores

-   One from each pair is assigned to lyrics; the other to no lyrics

-   Adding "randomness":

    -   It is randomly decided which person listens to which kind of music

-   Variability has been reduced by pairing like-individuals

## Why is "randomness" so important? {.center}

Randomness allows us to account for confounding variables!

-   Think back to chapter 4

-   These are different methods of **random assignment**

# Paired Designs

## Paired Designs {.center}

Response variables come in pairs, with one response value in the pair belonging to each explanatory variable group.

-   Two types of paired designs

## Types of Paired Designs {.center}

Repeated measures:

-   Measuring the same individual twice (once for each explanatory group)

Matched pairs:

-   Pairing two individuals based on similarities

-   One from each pair is assigned to each explanatory group

## Paired vs. Independent Design {.center}

Both attempt to answer the same research question

-   Independent design:

    -   Each individual is unrelated to others in the study

    -   Each observational/experimental unit gives only one response/doesn't have a counterpart

    -   Analyzing a difference in means

-   Paired design: Analyzing a mean difference

## Examples {.center}

Discuss with people around you if you think the designs are independent or paired

1.  Reaction times for students taken at 8 am compared to reaction times taken for the same students at 10 pm

2.  Change in weight for those on the Atkins Diet compared to change in weight for those on the Paleo Diet

3.  Time for skiers to complete a downhill race course on skis treated with wax A compared to skiers completing the same course on skis treated with wax B

## Why matched pairs? {.center}

Can get more informative results

-   By minimizing unit to unit difference, we can focus on **explanatory group** differences

-   Concept of "blocking" (beyond the scope of this class)

-   Must make sure design is correctly identified!

    -   Otherwise, analysis can be incorrect

## Teaching with Technology {.center style="font-size: 32px"}

Which example is an example of a paired design? Why?

1.  A teacher taught one class a lesson using technology and a different class a lesson without technology and then compared their quiz scores.

2.  A teacher taught a lesson using technology and then compared class scores to the national average score.

3.  A teacher teaches a lesson using technology and then gives her students a quiz and then compares those quiz scores to those from her class from the previous year.

4.  Pairs of students are matched by similar IQs. One in each pair is taught a lesson using technology and the other is taught without technology. Their quiz scores are compared.
